title: Naive Pattern Matching and KMP
summary: Substring search from O(nm) brute force to O(n+m) with the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm, built on a precomputed failure array that turns every mismatch into a smart jump instead of a restart.

slides.markdown:
Finding a pattern of length m inside a text of length n is a problem everyone can solve naively — slide the pattern across the text, compare at each position. That costs **O(n·m)** in the worst case, and "worst case" here isn't exotic: it happens on real, common inputs like `"aaaa...a"` searched for `"aaab"`.

**Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP)** gets the same answer in **O(n + m)**, guaranteed, by precomputing one array — the failure function — that tells you exactly how far to jump on a mismatch instead of restarting from scratch. The array is the whole trick; once you have it, the scan itself is almost identical to the naive one.

Brute force tries every starting position in the text, and at each one compares the pattern character by character until either a mismatch or a full match.

The waste: when a mismatch happens after matching, say, 5 characters, brute force throws away all 5 characters of information and restarts the comparison one position to the right, from scratch. But those 5 matched characters tell you something about the text — specifically, the text right there looks like a known prefix of the pattern. KMP's entire idea is refusing to discard that information.

The **LPS array** ("longest proper prefix which is also a suffix") is computed once, from the pattern alone, before any scanning starts. `lps[i]` is the length of the longest proper prefix of `pattern[0..i]` that is also a proper suffix of that same substring.

"Proper" means it can't be the whole substring itself — only a strictly shorter piece counts. For `pattern = "ababaca"`: `lps[3]` (looking at `"abab"`) is 2, because `"ab"` is both a prefix and a suffix of `"abab"`, and no longer match exists.

This array is exactly the information brute force throws away: it tells you, after any partial match, what prefix of the pattern is already guaranteed to be sitting in the text.

slides.sectionTitle: Building the LPS array on a repeating pattern
slides.markdown:
![The string ababaca with its LPS values below each index, and arrows from indices 2 and 3 back to the prefix they match](assets/kmp-lps-array-build.svg)

Watch how the array climbs during the repeating `"abab"` stretch (0, 0, 1, 2) as longer and longer prefixes reappear as suffixes, then drops sharply back to 0 at the `"c"` — a character that breaks the repetition entirely resets the count, because no suffix ending there can match any prefix anymore.

slides.sectionTitle: Computing the LPS array in O(m)
slides.markdown:
```python
def build_lps(pattern):
    m = len(pattern)
    lps = [0] * m
    length = 0          # length of the current matching prefix/suffix
    i = 1
    while i < m:
        if pattern[i] == pattern[length]:
            length += 1
            lps[i] = length
            i += 1
        elif length > 0:
            length = lps[length - 1]   # fall back using lps itself, don't restart from 0
        else:
            lps[i] = 0
            i += 1
    return lps
```

The subtlety: on a mismatch, `length` doesn't reset to 0 — it falls back to `lps[length - 1]`, reusing the array being built to skip redundant comparisons. That self-reference is what keeps this O(m) instead of O(m²).

slides.sectionTitle: The main scan: jump instead of restart
slides.markdown:
During the text scan, when `text[i] != pattern[j]` after some partial match, KMP does **not** move `i` back to retry from the next text position. Instead it sets `j = lps[j - 1]` — jump the pattern pointer back to the longest prefix that's guaranteed to already match — and retries the comparison at the same `i`.

`i` only ever moves forward, never backward. That single invariant is what gives KMP its O(n) bound on the text: each of the n text characters is compared a bounded number of times across the whole scan, not re-compared once per pattern restart.

The single most common KMP bug: using `lps[j]` instead of `lps[j - 1]` when falling back after a mismatch, or vice versa in `build_lps`. Because the array is 0-indexed but represents "length of a prefix," the fallback target for a match of length `j` is `lps[j - 1]` — the LPS value **of the last matched character**, not of the current position.

Getting this backwards doesn't crash — it silently returns wrong matches or misses real ones, and it's easy to not notice on a test string that happens not to exercise the fallback path. Test KMP specifically on a pattern with internal repetition (like `"aabaabaa"`) — that's the input shape that actually exercises the fallback logic and exposes an off-by-one.

slides.sectionTitle: KMP vs brute force vs a built-in search
slides.markdown:
| Approach | Worst case | When it actually matters |
|---|---|---|
| Brute force | O(n·m) | Fine for short patterns/text, or text known to be "random-like" |
| KMP | O(n + m), guaranteed | Adversarial or repetitive text (DNA sequences, log-scanning for a repeated token) |
| Language built-in (`str.find`, `strstr`) | Usually a tuned hybrid (often Boyer-Moore-ish or SIMD-accelerated) | The default choice in application code — don't hand-roll KMP unless the interview asks for it |

The honest interview answer: real code almost always calls the built-in. KMP earns its place when you need a **guaranteed** linear bound regardless of input shape — for example scanning network payloads for a signature where an adversary controls the input and could otherwise engineer brute force's O(n·m) worst case on purpose.

slides.sectionTitle: What the LPS array is really encoding
slides.markdown:
Step back and the LPS array is really answering one question for every prefix of the pattern: "if I'm partway through matching and hit a wall, what's the longest head-start I still have?" That head-start is a prefix of the pattern that's simultaneously a suffix of what you've already matched — meaning it's still sitting in the text, unconsumed, ready to continue matching from.

This is the same core idea reused across pattern-matching algorithms — you'll see it again with the Z-array (a different bookkeeping for the same substring-search power) and, later, in a different form, in Manacher's mirror trick for palindromes.
